lessons.title: What to monitor and why
lessons.html:
The purpose of monitoring

Natural resource management (NRM) practices, such as rotational grazing, contour banks, alien clearing and irrigation scheduling, only work if they are done properly and if their effects are checked. Monitoring means regularly observing and recording the condition of resources and the practices applied, so that problems are caught early and management can adjust.

Resources and indicators

ResourceWhat to monitor (indicators)
SoilErosion signs (rills, gullies, dongas, sheet erosion, exposed roots), soil cover percentage, compaction, soil test results over time
WaterRainfall, dam and borehole levels, water quality, irrigation volumes used, leaks, riverbank condition
Veld and pastureGrass cover and species composition, bare patches, bush encroachment, grazing days per camp, animal condition
BiodiversityPresence of wetlands, indigenous vegetation, pollinators, birds and wildlife; alien invasive plant spread
PracticesWhether contours are maintained, camps rotated on schedule, firebreaks prepared, chemicals stored and disposed of correctly

The legal side

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 places duties on land users to protect soil, water and vegetation and to control weeds and invader plants. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 governs water use and pollution. Monitoring helps a farm show it is meeting these obligations.

Baseline

To see change, you need a starting point. Record the condition at the start of a season or when a practice begins: photos from fixed points, veld assessments, soil test results and water levels.

lessons.title: Monitoring methods, recording and reporting
lessons.html:
Practical methods

  • Fixed-point photographs: mark a spot with a peg or post and take a photo in the same direction at the same time each year or season. Over time, photos show changes in cover, erosion or bush.
  • Field walks with a checklist: walk camps, lands and waterways on a schedule and tick off indicators.
  • Rain gauges and meters: read daily or as set and record.
  • Grazing charts: record which animals were in which camp, from which date to which date.
  • Veld condition assessments: done by trained staff or advisers using a standard method.
  • Soil and water tests: sampled and sent to a lab as scheduled.
  • Alien plant mapping: mark infestations on a farm map and track clearing.

Recording

Good records are dated, specific and kept in one place, on paper or in the farm system. For each observation note: date, location (camp or land name), what was seen, measurement if any, photo reference and who recorded it.

Interpreting results

Compare current observations with the baseline and targets. Examples:

  • Grass cover in Camp 5 has dropped compared with last year's photo: the camp may be overgrazed or under-rested.
  • A rill has formed below the contour bank: the bank may be broken or overtopped.
  • Borehole levels are falling each month in a dry year: water use may need to be reduced.

Reporting and corrective action

  • Report findings to the manager clearly, with location, evidence and urgency.
  • Suggest corrective actions, such as resting a camp, repairing a bank, scheduling alien clearing, or fixing leaks.
  • Follow up to check that the action was done and worked.

Safety

When monitoring alone in remote areas, tell someone your route and return time, carry a phone and water, and take care near dams, gullies and animals.

Key points

  • Monitoring checks whether NRM practices work and catches problems early.
  • Monitor soil, water, veld, biodiversity and the practices themselves.
  • Set a baseline and use fixed-point photos and checklists.
  • Record date, location, observation and evidence.
  • Report clearly, recommend actions and follow up.

quiz.question: Which is an indicator of soil erosion?

options.text: A photo of the farm owner

The camp may be overgrazed or under-rested
